title: Major Burn: First Aid, Fluids, and Escharotomy
description: Cool the burn with running water, refer to a burn center, resuscitate with balanced crystalloid titrated to urine output rather than the formula alone, release a compromised circumferential burn by escharotomy, and avoid prophylactic antibiotics.
objectives: Give effective burn first aid and recognize burn center referral criteria
Prescribe initial fluid resuscitation by weight and burn size
Titrate fluids to urine output and recognize fluid creep
Recognize a circumferential burn compromising the limb and release it by escharotomy

references.citation: European Burns Association. European Practice Guidelines for Burn Care: Minimum Level of Burn Care Provision in Europe. Version 4. Barcelona: European Burns Association; 2017.

Griffin BR, Frear CC, Babl F, et al. Cool Running Water First Aid Decreases Skin Grafting Requirements in Pediatric Burns: A Cohort Study of Two Thousand Four Hundred Ninety-five Children. Ann Emerg Med. 2020;75(1):75-85.
Saffle JI. The phenomenon of "fluid creep" in acute burn resuscitation. J Burn Care Res. 2007;28(3):382-395.

start.text: A 35-year-old man weighing 80 kg was pulled from a burning shed 40 minutes ago. He is talking normally. He has deep partial- and full-thickness burns of the chest, abdomen, and both arms, about 30% TBSA, including a full-thickness burn all the way around the left forearm. His burnt clothing is still on, and the burns have not been cooled.

first.text: Which belong in your first steps?

options.label: Remove burnt clothing that is not stuck, and any constricting jewelry
Cool running water on the burns for 20 minutes, while keeping him warm
Arrange transfer to a burn center
Ice packs, to cool the burns faster
A topical cream on the burns before transfer

first.feedback: EBA 2017: remove burnt clothing unless it is stuck, and any constricting jewelry. Cool with running water for 20 minutes, avoiding hypothermia; it helps within 3 hours of injury. Do not use ice, and avoid topical creams before transfer, as they hinder later wound assessment. Refer adults with superficial dermal burns over 20% TBSA, any deep partial- or full-thickness burn, circumferential burns, or a need for burn shock resuscitation to a burn center. In a cohort of 2,495 children, 20 minutes of cool running water within 3 hours lowered the odds of skin grafting (OR 0.6).

fluids.text: What fluid do you prescribe for the first 24 hours?

options.label: Balanced crystalloid such as Ringer's lactate, 2–4 mL/kg/%TBSA (4.8–9.6 L), half in the first 8 hours, titrated to urine output
options.feedback: EBA 2017: resuscitate adults with burns over 20% TBSA, prescribing 2 to 4 mL/kg/%TBSA over the first 24 hours with crystalloid as first line. Here that is 2–4 × 80 kg × 30% = 4,800–9,600 mL. Give half in the first 8 hours and half over the next 16, titrated to urine output. The Parkland (4 mL) and modified Brooke (2 mL) formulas bracket this range.

options.label: 0.9% saline at 4 mL/kg/%TBSA
options.feedback: EBA 2017 recommends against 0.9% saline for burn resuscitation. It is linked to hypernatremia, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, and a higher risk of acute kidney injury; balanced crystalloid is preferred.

options.label: Albumin from the start instead of crystalloid
options.feedback: EBA 2017: use crystalloid as first line, and avoid systematic use of colloids, which can be considered as salvage therapy. No colloids are given in the first 8 hours after the burn.

urine.text: Six hours in, his urine output is 130 mL/h (about 1.6 mL/kg/h), and he is hemodynamically stable. What do you do with the fluids?

options.label: Reduce the infusion rate, aiming for about 0.5 mL/kg/h of urine
options.feedback: EBA 2017: titrate crystalloid to urine output, targeting 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (1 mL/kg/h in children under 30 kg, 1–2 mL/kg/h in high-voltage burns), and reduce the rate once the endpoints are met. Over-resuscitation ('fluid creep') is linked to abdominal compartment syndrome, excess edema, respiratory failure, and acute kidney injury. Modern patients often receive far more fluid than the Parkland formula predicts.

options.label: Keep the calculated rate unchanged for the full 24 hours
options.feedback: EBA 2017: fluids are titrated to urine output, and the rate is reduced once the targets are met. Over-resuscitation ('fluid creep') is associated with abdominal compartment syndrome and other serious complications.

forearm.text: The circumferential left forearm burn is now tight. His hand is cool, capillary refill is slow, and he has tingling in his fingers. Next?

options.label: Escharotomy by an experienced clinician, with mid-axial incisions from normal skin to normal skin; fasciotomy only if compression persists
options.feedback: EBA 2017: perform escharotomy when a circumferential burn compromises circulation, by a suitably experienced clinician. Make full-thickness incisions down to fat along the mid-axial lines, from normal skin to normal skin, near but not directly over the nerves and vessels; on the hand, incisions go on the dorsum. Fasciotomy is rarely a primary procedure outside high-voltage or very deep burns, and is indicated when compression persists after escharotomy.

options.label: Forearm fasciotomy as the first procedure
options.feedback: EBA 2017: apart from high-voltage electrical injuries and very deep burns, fasciotomy is rarely a primary procedure in burns. It is indicated when compression persists after escharotomy, and it carries a higher risk of neurovascular injury.

options.label: Elevate the arm and review in the morning
options.feedback: EBA 2017: elevation reduces edema, but escharotomy is recommended when a circumferential burn compromises circulation. Color, capillary refill, pulses, pain, and paresthesia should be checked at regular intervals.

closure.text: His limb perfusion recovers after escharotomy. What is your wound plan?

options.label: Aim for early wound closure, without prophylactic systemic antibiotics
options.feedback: EBA 2017: a longer time to healing is linked to hypertrophic scarring, so aim to close burn wounds as soon as possible. Prophylactic systemic antibiotics are not supported by evidence.

options.label: Prophylactic IV antibiotics to prevent burn wound infection
options.feedback: EBA 2017: the use of prophylactic systemic antibiotics in burn care is not supported by evidence.

fail_first.text: Guideline Deviation: Burn first aid or referral not by the guideline.

fail_fluids.text: Guideline Deviation: Resuscitation fluid against the guideline.

fail_limb.text: Complication: Limb ischemia under a circumferential burn.

fail_antibiotics.text: Guideline Deviation: Prophylactic antibiotics without evidence.

success.text: Case Complete: Burn cooled, referred, resuscitated, and released.
